words.note: Nationality ends -ian: Brazil + ian = Brazilian.

flag.text: You wrote Brazilion with -ion. It is -ian, like Italian and Canadian.

words.note: Denmark → Danish: the word loses "-mark" and e becomes a.
Finland has one n — but Finnish has two.
Greece (country, -ce) → Greek (person, -k). Irregular!
Hungary ends -ary (like January), not -ery.
Lebanon (country) → Lebanese (person).

flag.text: The book lists the language as "Lebanese". There is no Lebanese language — people in Lebanon speak Arabic (and often French/English). Lebanese is only the nationality.

words.note: Ma-lay-sia — hidden inside it is the language, Malay.

flag.text: You wrote P instead of L twice. It is Malaysia and Malaysian.

words.note: The person is a New Zealander (informally a "Kiwi"). Language: English (and Māori).
Gulf countries usually add just -i: Omani, Qatari, Iraqi.
Country = Philippines (Ph, one L, double P). Person = Filipino (F, one L, one P). A woman is a Filipina.

flag.text: Two slips: you doubled the L (it is one L, then double P), and the person is spelled with F: Filipino. Your third column also needs the language, which is Filipino.

words.note: One R at the front, double S in the middle: R-u-ss-i-a.

flag.text: You started with two Rs. Only one R: Russian.
The book lists the language as "South Korean". The language is simply Korean — the "South" only describes the country and the people.

words.note: Thailand = Thai + land. Nothing is added for the nationality: Thai.
Same pattern as Kazakhstan → Kazakh. "Uzbekistani" is also correct.

flag.text: The row was left half-written. Nationality = Uzbek, language = Uzbek.

words.en: a family with four people in it
words.ex: We are a family of four: my parents, my brother and me.

words.en: unusual and interesting, from a faraway country
words.vi: kỳ lạ, mang nét ngoại lai
words.ex: The market was full of exotic fruit I had never seen before.
words.note: One x, no k: e-x-o-tic.

words.en: assist somebody, especially when they are busy or in trouble
words.vi: giúp đỡ ai (khi họ gặp khó)
words.ex: Could you help me out with the washing-up?

flag.text: Handwriting slip — the phrase is help somebody out (help sb out).

words.en: start doing something again after a break
words.vi: quay lại làm gì sau một thời gian nghỉ
words.ex: After the exams I want to get back into swimming.
words.note: Write into as one word here, not "in to".

words.en: relax completely (informal)
words.ex: At the weekend I just chill out with my friends.
words.note: Double L: chill out.

words.en: be very enthusiastic about something; like it a lot
words.ex: My mum is very keen on volleyball.
words.note: k-ee-n (like "seen"). Next verb takes -ing: keen on playing.

words.en: think of an idea, plan or answer
words.ex: She came up with a brilliant idea for the project.

flag.wrote: come up with = have a good idea
flag.right: come up with = think of an idea, plan or answer
flag.text: Close, but the idea does not have to be good — and you can also come up with a plan, an excuse or an answer. Better: think of or produce an idea or solution.

words.en: leave a bus, train or plane (also: to start a journey)
words.ex: We get off at the next stop.

flag.right: get off = leave a bus / train / plane
flag.text: "Depart" is only half of it. The everyday FCE meaning is to leave a bus / train / plane — the opposite of get on. (For a plane you also "get off"; for a car it is get out of.)

words.en: solve a problem or calculate an answer
words.ex: I could not work out the answer to question 5.

words.en: disappoint somebody; fail to do what you promised
words.ex: You can trust Ana — she will never let you down.
words.note: The noun is a let-down. And note: "make somebody disappointed" needs the -ed.

words.en: depend on; trust somebody to do something
words.ex: I rely on my sister to wake me up.
words.note: rely → relies, relied, reliable: the y becomes i.

words.en: argue with somebody and stop being friends
words.vi: cãi nhau và mất lòng nhau
words.ex: They fell out with each other over a silly joke.
words.note: Past tense: fell out with. Noun: a falling-out.

words.en: like each other as soon as you meet
words.ex: We hit it off straight away and became best friends.
words.note: The it never changes: we hit it off, they hit it off.

words.en: resemble an older member of your family
words.ex: Elena takes after her mother — they have the same eyes.

flag.text: The book gave "resemble" to the wrong phrasal verb. The verb that means resemble a relative is take after somebody. Look out for means to watch out for / protect. Learn the pair together.

words.en: organise something; deal with a problem successfully
words.vi: sắp xếp, giải quyết cho xong
words.ex: I need to sort out my school bag before Monday.

flag.text: They overlap but are not the same. Work out = calculate or find the answer. Sort out = tidy / organise, or fix a practical problem.

words.en: fail to meet somebody you arranged to meet
words.vi: cho ai leo cây (không đến chỗ hẹn)
words.ex: He stood me up — I waited outside the cinema for an hour!
words.note: Past tense: stood somebody up.

flag.text: You wrote out. It is stand somebody UP. ("Stand out" exists but means be noticeable — a completely different phrase.)

words.en: go to the station or airport to say goodbye to somebody
words.ex: We went to the airport to see my cousin off.

words.en: do the same job or the same thing as somebody before you
words.vi: nối gót, theo bước chân của ai
words.ex: She followed in her father’s footsteps and became a doctor.
words.note: footsteps = one word, always plural. Keep the apostrophe: somebody’s.

flag.right: follow in sb's footsteps = follow the same career/path
flag.text: "Imitate" is too wide — it can mean copying anyone. This phrase is specifically about following the same career or path as somebody in your family.

words.en: turn your eyes towards something
words.ex: Look at this photo of my grandmother.

words.en: try to find something
words.ex: I am looking for my pencil case.

words.en: be careful — watch for danger
words.ex: Look out — there is a car coming!

words.en: watch and take care of somebody; keep your eyes open for them
words.vi: trông chừng, để ý bảo vệ ai
words.ex: Big brothers should look out for their little sisters.

flag.right: look out for = watch for / protect
flag.text: Wrong meaning in the book. Look out for = watch for / protect. The one that means resemble is take after somebody.

words.en: take care of somebody or something
words.ex: I look after my little brother on Fridays.

flag.text: "Mong chờ" belongs to look forward to. Look after = chăm sóc (take care of).

words.en: look the same as each other
words.ex: My mum and I look alike.
words.note: alike is one word and comes after the people: they look alike.

words.en: investigate something; examine it carefully
words.ex: The teacher promised to look into the problem.

flag.right: look into = điều tra, xem xét
flag.text: "Nhìn vào" is look at. Look into = điều tra / xem xét (investigate).

words.en: feel happy and excited about something that is going to happen
words.ex: I am looking forward to the summer holidays.
words.note: The next verb takes -ing: look forward to seeing you.

flag.right: look forward to = mong chờ, háo hức
flag.text: "Hồi hộp" means nervous / tense. Look forward to is positive: mong chờ, háo hức.

words.en: admire and respect somebody
words.ex: I look up to my grandmother — she is so brave.

words.en: think you are better than somebody; despise them
words.ex: Never look down on people who are different from you.

words.en: recall something; think again about a past moment
words.ex: Let us look back at what we learned last week.

words.en: reminisce — remember a whole period of your life
words.ex: I will look back on these school years and smile.
words.note: look back at a moment or detail · look back on a whole period.

words.en: willing to work together and help
words.ex: She is very cooperative in group work.
words.note: Double o: c-oo-perative. Opposite adds un-.

words.en: behaving in a sensible, grown-up way
words.ex: He is very mature for a fifteen-year-old.
words.note: Opposite takes im-, not un-: immature. Also the opposite of childish.

words.en: kind — thinks about what other people need
words.ex: What a thoughtful present!

flag.text: You dropped the t. It comes from thought: thoughtful / thoughtless.

words.en: showing that you understand and care about somebody’s problems
words.ex: My teacher was very sympathetic when I was ill.
words.note: Starts sym- with a y, then -pa-thetic.

words.en: puts a lot of effort into work
words.ex: Elena is a hard-working student.
words.note: Usually written with a hyphen. The opposite is lazy — there is no "un-" form.

words.en: can be trusted to do what they promise
words.ex: He is the most reliable person on the team.
words.note: From rely: rely → reliable (y→i), ending -able.

flag.text: The letters got tangled. Build it in pieces: un + reli + able = unreliable.

words.en: full of energy; very active
words.ex: My grandfather is more energetic than me!
words.note: Noun: energy → adjective energetic (the stress moves to -GET-).

flag.text: "Unenergetic" is not natural English. Use not very energetic, lazy, or (more formal) lethargic.

words.en: able to wait calmly without getting annoyed
words.ex: You must be patient with young children.
words.note: Ends -tient. Opposite takes im-. Noun: patience.

flag.text: Small slip in the Vietnamese too — it is kiên nhẫn.

words.en: can be trusted to do the right thing
words.ex: She is responsible for locking the classroom.
words.note: Ends -sible, not -sable. Opposite takes ir-.

flag.text: Only one e at the end: irresponsible.

words.en: showing a lot of excitement and interest
words.ex: The class was enthusiastic about the trip.
words.note: en-thu-si-as-tic. Noun: enthusiasm. Same idea as be keen on.

words.en: aware of other people’s feelings; also easily upset
words.ex: Be careful — he is quite sensitive about his height.
words.note: Opposite takes in-: insensitive.

flag.text: You dropped the n. Say it in syllables: sen-si-tive.

words.en: kind and looking after other people
words.ex: Nurses are usually very caring people.
words.note: care → caring: drop the e before -ing.

words.en: plans well and keeps things tidy
words.ex: Keep your notes organised and revision is easy.
words.note: British -ised, American -ized — both accepted in the exam. Opposite: disorganised.

words.en: slightly rude or disrespectful, but often in a funny way
words.ex: That was a cheeky answer to give your teacher!
words.note: Spelling: ch-eek-y (like "cheek", your face).

flag.text: "Láu cá" means sly or crafty — that is sly / crafty / cunning. Cheeky is cheerfully rude: nghịch ngợm, hơi hỗn. It is often affectionate.

words.en: always finding faults in other people
words.ex: Try not to be too critical of your friends.
words.note: Ends -cal. Verb: criticise. Noun: criticism.

flag.text: "Uncritical" exists, but it means accepting things without questioning them — it is not the natural opposite of a critical person. For personality, use complimentary, encouraging or supportive.

words.en: annoying; making you feel impatient
words.vi: gây khó chịu, làm người khác bực
words.ex: His habit of tapping the desk is really irritating.
words.note: Double r: i-rr-i-ta-ting. Verb: irritate.

flag.text: "Non-irritating" is used for creams and shampoo, not people. The opposite of an irritating person is pleasant, easy-going or soothing.

words.en: behaving like a young child (a criticism)
words.ex: Stop being childish and apologise.
words.note: child + ish. Careful: childlike is positive (innocent); childish is negative.

words.en: an area you study at school, e.g. maths, history
words.ex: My favourite subject is English.

words.en: the tool you use to draw circles (also: for finding north)
words.ex: Use a compass to draw a perfect circle.
words.note: Double s. In maths you can also say a pair of compasses.

words.en: a small machine for doing sums
words.ex: You cannot use a calculator in this test.

flag.text: Two slips: the missing c (cal-cu-la-tor) and the ending — it is -or, not -er.

words.en: a small bag you keep pens and pencils in
words.ex: My pencil case is full of broken pencils.

flag.text: It is pen-cil (like the pencil you write with) — and two separate words.

words.en: the tool that makes a pencil point sharp
words.ex: Has anybody got a pencil sharpener?

flag.text: Tools like this usually end -er: sharpener. (But calculator ends -or — these two are worth learning as a pair.)

words.en: the thing you use to remove pencil marks (US: eraser)
words.ex: Can I borrow your rubber? I made a mistake.

flag.text: Double b: rubber. British English = rubber, American English = eraser.

words.en: the special clothes all students at a school wear
words.ex: We have to wear a uniform at my school.
words.note: uni = one + form = shape. One n, no double letters.

words.en: the bag you carry your books to school in
words.ex: My schoolbag weighs a ton on Mondays.

words.en: dress yourself in something
words.ex: Put on your uniform — we are late!
words.note: put on = the action of dressing · wear = the state of having it on.

extraFlags.text: The heading of the first column. A county is a region inside a country (like a province). A country is Vietnam, Italy, Japan…
aux-il-i-ary. Two is in the middle: auxiliary.
Ends -ue: argue. Noun: an argument (careful — no e in argument!).
The adjective needs the full -ed: disappointed. One s, double p.

reference.title: Nationality endings — the four patterns
rows: Brazil→Brazilian · Italy→Italian · Hungary→Hungarian · Russia→Russian · Canada→Canadian · Malaysia→Malaysian · Australia→Australian
